title: The Middle Assyrian world beyond its kings
summary: How Assyria grew from its Tigris heartland into a territorial kingdom, and how farming, families and provincial offices sustained it.

sections.title: A kingdom extending west from Ashur
sections.text:
The Middle Assyrian period, broadly about 1500-1000 BCE in the ATMAP project's chronology, saw a state centred on Ashur expand westwards across northern Mesopotamia. Ashur stood on the Tigris in what is now Iraq; the Habur valley, farther west in present-day Syria, became an important region of provincial government. This was the second millennium BCE, centuries before the campaigns of Sennacherib familiar from Kings and Isaiah.

Expansion changed the scale of government. Ruling beyond the capital required provincial officials, agricultural resources and written communication between settlements. During the thirteenth century BCE, Shalmaneser I and Tukulti-Ninurta I ruled a kingdom whose western administration is particularly visible at Dur-Katlimmu. The city and its surrounding countryside helped turn territorial claims into organised supplies and labour.

sections.title: Cities, fields and provincial stores
sections.text:
Dur-Katlimmu lay on the lower Habur, at modern Tell Sheikh Hamad. Its offices connected government to rural production: crops and herds had to be managed, goods accounted for and people supplied. Agricultural records from the city name barley, wheat and sesame, while livestock accounts concern cattle, donkeys and smaller stock. The kingdom's resources included the products of fields and animals as well as the people who worked with them.

This relationship explains why a provincial centre mattered beyond its walls. A court or official household could direct resources produced in the surrounding landscape. The excavated accounts describe particular institutional estates, however, rather than every farm or family in the valley.

sections.title: Families and unequal legal standing
sections.text:
Middle Assyrian society distinguished people by freedom, household position, sex and marital standing. The law collection's veiling provisions make these divisions visible: some women were required to cover their heads in public, while enslaved women and women conventionally translated as prostitutes were forbidden to do so. The veil could mark a recognised social position, rather than a rule applied uniformly to all women.

Households were also centres of economic action. Contemporary deeds discussed by Frederick Mario Fales show women entering contracts for absent husbands, lending, borrowing, adopting and purchasing. These activities sit alongside legal prescriptions that place women under male authority. The history therefore includes both unequal power and documented opportunities for women to act.

sections.title: Writing made obligations durable
sections.text:
A receipt turned a transfer into something an official could consult later. KAJ 233 from Ashur, for example, records barley received by Anu-shumu-erish for service horses. Another tablet, MARV 10, 07, records a pair of palace shoes assigned to Niri-shaldi, described in the edition as a hostage, under a steward's responsibility. These are small transactions, but they show how resources and people were placed within chains of accountability.

The modern ATMAP corpus contains more than 3,000 cuneiform pieces. Within that larger collection, individual receipts, letters and legal documents reveal different parts of administration. Their value for social history lies in the particular obligations they preserve, not simply in the size of the collection.

sections.title: Asshur and Assyrian cities in Scripture
sections.text:
Genesis 10:8-12 and 10:22 provide biblical accounts of Asshur and named cities. Genesis 10:11-12 places Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah and Resen within its account of the region; Genesis 10:22 includes Asshur among the sons of Shem. These passages give the archive's biblical starting points for those names and relationships.

The Assyrian conquest described in 2 Kings 17:3-6 is a later episode: Hoshea's kingdom falls after the siege of Samaria, and Israelites are carried away to named destinations. Reading the passages in sequence helps distinguish the Bible's origins material from its accounts of the later territorial empire. Neither passage supplies the names or transactions in a thirteenth-century provincial receipt.

title: Provincial offices and Dūr-Katlimmu
summary: How Dur-Katlimmu's officials managed western Assyria through correspondence, agricultural accounts and sealed documents.

sections.title: A provincial centre on the Habur
sections.text:
Dūr-Katlimmu, identified with Tell Sheikh Hamad on the lower Habur, served as an important western administrative centre during the reigns of Shalmaneser I and Tukulti-Ninurta I in the thirteenth century BCE. Its location placed an Assyrian office within the agricultural landscape of what is now north-eastern Syria, away from the royal and religious centre at Ashur.

The city mattered because western rule required continuing management after military expansion. Officials needed to handle supplies, personnel and correspondence. The archaeological and written evidence makes Dur-Katlimmu a place where the workings of a territorial kingdom can be studied at the level of an office and its records.

sections.title: Building P and its records
sections.text:
Excavators recovered 666 registered fragmentary cuneiform tablets in a sealed deposit in room A of Building P, according to the Harvard-hosted glyptic research report. Thousands of clay sealing devices accompanied the tablets. The complex is interpreted as a chancellery associated with an adjoining, unexcavated palace. It was a setting for handling documents and controlled goods, not merely a store of literary texts.

The physical association matters: tablets carried written statements, while seal impressions supplied another means of identifying or controlling administrative acts. The recorded total belongs to this report's deposit and registration history. Other publications organise and count the site's written finds differently, so their totals should not be silently combined.

sections.title: Who exercised authority
sections.text:
The western administrative centre was headed by a grand vizier. The glyptic project identifies the seal of Shulmanu-mushabshi, a holder of that office, and a seal of the district governor Etir-Marduk. These titles show that provincial government included several ranks rather than a single official acting in isolation. Seal images made office and authority visible on the material used in administration.

Agricultural management formed another level. At Dur-Katlimmu, overseers of ploughmen directed cultivators and received personnel, draught animals and ration grain from the palace. The link between a high office, an agricultural supervisor and the people doing fieldwork helps explain how government reached into rural production, although surviving records do not provide a complete organisation chart.

sections.title: What an office needed to account for
sections.text:
Institutional farming required officials to account for land, crops and animals. Dur-Katlimmu's records include the commissioning of herders and their later accounting for flocks, as well as the yields of cultivated fields. Responsibility continued after an initial assignment: animals and produce had to be related back to the person charged with them.

A comparable chain appears in KAJ 233 at Ashur. The receipt names a quantity of barley, identifies its purpose as a ration for service horses and names the recipient and his father. Such details made a transfer distinguishable from another transfer. The two sites provide examples of accountable administration within the same broad period, rather than proof that every office used identical procedures.

sections.title: Letters connected provincial households
sections.text:
Government and household communication could overlap. A Middle Assyrian letter from Tell Taban, TabT05A-134, is addressed by Lulayu to Labe'tu, whom he calls his lady. It reports on people's wellbeing, a meeting involving Ili-pada and arrangements for medicine and divination. At the end, Lulayu requests supplies and asks for his correspondent's instructions.

This example gives provincial correspondence a human dimension. A letter could carry news about illness while also coordinating resources and maintaining a relationship of authority. Tell Taban and Dur-Katlimmu are separate archives, but together they show why provincial history includes households and personal communication alongside accounts and official titles.

title: Women, status and the Middle Assyrian Laws
summary: Who could veil, how marriage affected status and inheritance, what penalties the laws prescribed, and how women acted in contracts and household affairs.

sections.title: What the laws are
sections.text:
The Middle Assyrian Laws survive in a set of cuneiform tablets from Ashur, rather than a complete legal code comparable to a modern statute book. Their provisions describe particular situations and the consequences to follow. Tablet A contains 59 provisions dealing largely with women and household relations, including marriage, property, sexual offences, accusations, veiling and debts. Tablet B addresses inheritance, farming and irrigation; Tablet C+G concerns pledges and deposits.

The surviving copies also have a history. Fales describes the collection as largely preserved in eleventh-century BCE copies of earlier material. That distinction separates the date of a surviving tablet from the possible age of its rules. The laws show a strongly unequal social order in which freedom, marital position and male household authority affected legal treatment. They prescribe outcomes; they do not count how often a court imposed them.

sections.title: Veiling as a marker of status
sections.text:
Tablet A, provision 40, required wives and widows, and the free Assyrian women described in the rule, to cover their heads when appearing in the street. A concubine accompanying her mistress was also to be veiled. Enslaved women and women conventionally translated as prostitutes were forbidden to veil. Head covering therefore distinguished permitted public status as well as regulating dress.

Provision 41 connects veiling to a change in household standing. A man could assemble five or six companions, veil his concubine before them and declare her his wife. The witnesses and declaration made the change publicly recognisable. A woman who had not undergone that act remained a concubine under the rule. Veiling here was part of a legal procedure, not simply an expression of private belief. Fales also discusses a category called qadiltu whose precise occupation remains uncertain; it should not be assigned a confident modern equivalent.

sections.title: Marriage, inheritance and violent penalties
sections.text:
Provision 41 also addresses succession: if a man died without sons of his veiled wife, the sons of concubines were to receive an inheritance share. The rule shows why distinctions within a household had practical consequences. It also prevents the assumption that every child of a concubine was excluded from inheritance.

The penalties attached to prohibited veiling were severe. Provision 40 prescribes fifty blows and pitch poured over the head of a woman classed as a prostitute who veiled; for an enslaved woman it prescribes the cutting off of her ears. Men who saw a prohibited veil and failed to bring the woman before the authorities could themselves face corporal punishment and a month of royal service. These provisions attempted to enforce social boundaries through public denunciation and violence. They describe the collection's prescribed response, not a demonstrated record of every woman's treatment.

sections.title: Women in contracts and household affairs
sections.text:
Contemporary legal deeds reveal forms of action that the punitive provisions do not explain. Fales notes women contracting in the name of absent husbands, granting or requesting loans, adopting and purchasing. These are specific capacities within documented transactions. They do not establish equal rights for all women, but they show that a history confined to restrictions would omit important economic activity.

A provincial letter supplies a named example of a woman within a network of resources and instructions. In TabT05A-134, Lulayu addresses Labe'tu as his lady, discusses medicine and asks her to send what she has available and communicate her instructions. The letter concerns an elite setting and cannot stand for every household. It nevertheless lets the reader see a woman as a correspondent with a practical role, rather than only as the subject of a law.

sections.title: Marriage and remarriage in Deuteronomy
sections.text:
Deuteronomy 24:1-4 describes a man issuing a certificate of divorce, the woman leaving his house and marrying another man. If the second marriage ends through divorce or the second husband's death, the first husband is forbidden to take her back. The passage's focus is that prohibited return after an intervening marriage.

This differs from the Middle Assyrian provisions discussed above, which use veiling, witnessed declaration and household status to regulate particular relationships and inheritance. Both traditions treat marriage as having consequences beyond a couple's private wishes, but their actual rules must be stated separately. Deuteronomy supplies the primary biblical account of this remarriage restriction; it does not establish that Assyrian women followed the same procedure or that one text borrowed from the other.

title: Households, property and inheritance
summary: Marriage, inheritance shares, loans and the people who made a Middle Assyrian household an economic and legal institution.

sections.title: Marriage created different household positions
sections.text:
A Middle Assyrian household could contain people with different legal positions. The law collection distinguishes a wife from a concubine, and it also recognises enslaved women. These categories affected public appearance and the way a relationship could be acknowledged. Under Tablet A, provision 41, a man who wished to establish his concubine as a wife assembled five or six companions, veiled her before them and made a declaration.

The procedure made recognition a witnessed act. It gave other people a basis for distinguishing a wife from a woman who continued to hold the position of concubine. Household history therefore includes public legal relationships as well as domestic life, and the written rules place the power to make this particular declaration with the man.

sections.title: Children and an inheritance share
sections.text:
The same provision describes what happened when a man died without sons of his veiled wife: sons of concubines were recognised as sons who could receive the inheritance share. The presence or absence of sons in one household category changed the position of sons in another. The rule links marriage status, recognised parentage and the transfer of property after death.

It does not supply a complete table of shares for every possible family. In particular, this clause should not be expanded into a claim about all daughters, all widows or every adopted child. Its concrete contribution is narrower and useful: concubinage did not automatically exclude a man's sons from succession in the situation the provision describes.

sections.title: Women could arrange transactions
sections.text:
Household resources could be managed by women as well as men. In his discussion of contemporary legal deeds, Fales identifies women acting for absent husbands, making or requesting loans, adopting and purchasing. Those transactions required women to appear as parties with practical responsibilities and interests. An absent spouse did not mean that every economic decision in a household simply stopped.

This evidence complicates the impression created by laws that emphasise a husband's or father's authority. Fales suggests that the particularly restrictive norms may reflect the environment of the capital, while provincial practice was more varied. That explanation remains an interpretation. The documented activities themselves provide the stronger basis for describing women's economic participation without claiming universal legal equality.

sections.title: Documents recorded transfers and obligations
sections.text:
Property arrangements needed records that could identify what had changed hands and who was responsible. ATMAP's catalogues distinguish types such as receipts, allocations, lists and sale transactions. At Tell Taban, the Middle Assyrian entries include two documents catalogued as purchases of enslaved people, each with an envelope, alongside letters and accounts. This makes coercive ownership part of the household economy visible, even though catalogue labels alone do not recover the purchased individuals' lives.

An envelope gave a transaction an additional physical layer of documentation. The flour document TabT05A-151+ preserves both a tablet and an envelope repeating the receipt's central details. It concerns an institutional transfer rather than an inheritance, but shows the documentary form through which obligations could be retained.

sections.title: Illness and supplies crossed household boundaries
sections.text:
The letter TabT05A-134 shows an elite household participating in a wider social network. Lulayu writes to Labe'tu with reports of wellbeing and a meeting involving Ili-pada. His message turns to an illness, treatment with a herb and the scheduling of divination. He then asks his correspondent to send available supplies and promises to gather what is missing.

The practical picture is one of communication and co-operation: a household could be a point from which instructions and materials travelled. Health, authority and resource management appear in the same message. It is not a complete biography of Labe'tu, but it provides a particular event through which readers can understand household activity beyond an abstract list of legal categories.

title: Fields, irrigation and livestock
summary: The crops, herds, water systems and seasonal obligations that sustained farming around Dur-Katlimmu and the lower Habur.

sections.title: Farming depended on location and water
sections.text:
Farming in northern Mesopotamia combined cultivation sustained by rainfall with areas where access to river water made a substantial difference. The lower Habur lay toward the drier part of this landscape. Water supply helped determine which fields could be worked reliably and how intensively institutions could cultivate them.

Hervé Reculeau's study places Middle Assyrian irrigation within the expansion of royal investment in the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BCE. It distinguishes the canals associated with Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta in the east from developments in the lower Habur to the west. These were different settings within the kingdom. Irrigation increased the possibilities of cultivation, but required construction and continued maintenance rather than delivering abundance by itself.

sections.title: Barley, wheat and sesame
sections.text:
Dur-Katlimmu's agricultural documents name barley, wheat and sesame. Crop accounts measured the produce institutions expected to receive and allowed harvests to be compared. Wolfgang Röllig's edition of 106 written finds brings these records together with accounts of livestock management. They concern production administered around a provincial centre during the reigns of Shalmaneser I and Tukulti-Ninurta I.

The crop names give readers a more concrete picture than a general reference to grain. Cereals and sesame were separate products requiring accounting, and harvests varied. The records concern particular managed land, so they do not amount to a complete description of what every household grew or ate.

sections.title: Herds required accountable herders
sections.text:
The livestock records describe herders being commissioned and later accounting for the animals entrusted to them. Cattle, donkeys and smaller livestock formed distinct parts of the managed stock. The herder's responsibility connected animals outside the settlement to the office that kept the account.

Such arrangements made animal management an ongoing relationship. An initial assignment had to be followed by a return or accounting, rather than disappearing from the record once the animals left. This is a documented feature of institutional husbandry at Dur-Katlimmu, not a modern reconstruction of every herder's seasonal route. The texts reveal supervision and responsibility more clearly than they reveal a full day in a herder's life.

sections.title: Cultivators and their supervisors
sections.text:
Middle Assyrian agricultural personnel included ploughmen who actually cultivated land and overseers responsible for their work. At Dur-Katlimmu, the overseers received personnel, draught animals and ration grain from the palace. Organising cultivation therefore involved people, animal power and supplies together. The distinction between cultivator and supervisor is important: a title did not always describe someone physically doing the same task.

Canal work added another demand on labour. Reculeau distinguishes continuing investments in agricultural personnel from the digging and cleaning of canals, which drew on compulsory service. The institutional farm was consequently more than a field and its crop; it was a set of obligations that made cultivation possible.

sections.title: Harvests were vulnerable to disruption
sections.text:
Fields did not yield a stable surplus every year. The Dur-Katlimmu records describe production affected by hostile action and storms as well as water availability. These pressures could interrupt cultivation or reduce what an institution received. A regional centre could command labour and maintain accounts, but could not remove the risks of farming.

The Middle Assyrian Laws also treat agriculture and irrigation as matters requiring rules: Tablet B groups them with inheritance. This combination shows why land was both a productive resource and a legal concern. Families and institutions depended on its continuing use. The surviving accounts and laws illuminate that dependence from different directions, without providing a single guaranteed yield for the whole kingdom.

title: Workers, rations and compulsory service
summary: Named receipts show how food, footwear, temple work and compulsory obligations connected people to Middle Assyrian institutions.

sections.title: Supplying workers and service animals
sections.text:
Middle Assyrian institutions distributed resources for specific purposes rather than treating every allocation as an undifferentiated food ration. KAJ 233, a receipt from Ashur, records 16 homer and 5 seah of barley received by Anu-shumu-erish, son of Siniya, for the horse or horses associated with Parparrayu's service obligation. The edition preserves uncertainty over the number of horses; the quantity is not a daily ration for one animal.

The receipt names the recipient, purpose and date. Its barley supported an animal connected to service, showing that an institution's supply commitments extended beyond human food. The ancient units are retained here because converting them to a modern weight would require assumptions about capacity and grain density.

sections.title: A pair of shoes for a hostage
sections.text:
MARV 10, 07 records a pair of shoes belonging to the palace. They were under the responsibility of Apliya, the great steward, and were assigned to Niri-shaldi, whom the edition identifies as a hostage. The document links a named person, an item of clothing and an official responsible for the transfer.

Its wording also refers to the Euphrates and the lands of Tummi and Nairi in a passage interpreted, with a question mark, as a campaign setting. The certain administrative relationship should be distinguished from that uncertain reconstruction. Providing footwear did not establish that Niri-shaldi was free to leave; the designation hostage places the transaction within a relationship of political constraint.

sections.title: Temple work and compulsory service
sections.text:
KAJ 247 from Ashur mentions a group of 22 people, a banquet, a temple and named people responsible for the entry. Jacob Jan de Ridder's edition tentatively identifies the group as corvée workers and tentatively classifies the document as a receipt. Corvée means labour owed as an obligation, rather than freely negotiated employment. Because the reading is uncertain here, the record cannot establish the group's exact legal status.

The document nevertheless places organised personnel within a temple-related activity. It also refers to a writing-board, connecting a surviving clay record with another form of record keeping. Work, food-related events and religious institutions could meet within the same administrative transaction.

sections.title: Flour moved through an institutional account
sections.text:
At Tell Taban, TabT05A-151+ records flour under Tehup-sheni's responsibility received by Ashur-ketta-leshir. It distinguishes quantities and kinds of flour, rather than simply recording food. The document survives with an envelope that repeats the main receipt, giving the transaction an outer written record as well as the tablet itself.

Its continuation mentions several possible destinations or purposes, including the king, named towns and a meal associated with the king's daughter. The edition marks uncertainty about how these uses were included in the earlier total. The account therefore shows institutional provisioning across several demands, but does not justify assigning a specific meal allowance to every worker.

sections.title: Obligation took different forms
sections.text:
These records describe different relationships to institutions. Anu-shumu-erish receives barley for service horses; Apliya oversees the issue of palace footwear to a hostage; the temple-related entry may concern compulsory workers; and a provincial flour account distributes responsibility between named officials. They should not all be translated into the single modern category of an employee receiving wages.

The legal collection supplies another form of service: in its veiling provisions, a man punished for failing to report a prohibited veil could be required to perform a month of the king's service. Labour could thus appear as an administrative obligation or a prescribed penalty. The documents make those differences visible even where workers' own accounts have not survived.

title: Scribes, seals and the making of archives
summary: How Middle Assyrian scribes recorded quantities, dated transactions, protected tablets and used seals to identify authority.

sections.title: Scribes recorded a transaction in ordered detail
sections.text:
A short Middle Assyrian receipt could preserve enough information to distinguish one delivery from another. KAJ 233 begins with a quantity of barley, then gives its purpose, the recipient and his father's name. It ends with a month, day and eponym year. The record's structure connected goods to people and time.

These details made a transaction available for later checking. A scribe did not need to tell the whole story of the recipient's life to establish an accountable transfer. MARV 10, 07 similarly identifies palace footwear, the steward responsible and the person receiving it. Scribal work converted a practical handover into a lasting institutional record.

sections.title: Dates used named eponym years
sections.text:
The date on KAJ 233 gives the month Kuzallu, the thirteenth day and the eponymy of Adad-nirari. An eponym year was identified by a named official rather than by a number in the BCE system used today. Converting such a date into a modern year therefore depends on reconstructing the sequence of eponyms and the reigns to which they belong.

MARV 10, 07 uses the same broad dating form but names Adad-resha-ishi as its eponym. A matching personal name is not by itself enough to equate two dates or identify an official with a king. The tablets preserve the ancient date statement; an absolute modern date requires a separate chronological argument.

sections.title: Seals made authority visible
sections.text:
A seal could leave an identifying image in clay. At Dur-Katlimmu, excavators recovered seal impressions on tablets and on clay devices associated with an administrative deposit. The glyptic study identifies impressions connected to different levels of authority, including the grand vizier Shulmanu-mushabshi and the district governor Etir-Marduk. The material connects office holders to the physical handling of records and goods.

The Harvard-supported Dūr-Katlimmu research identifies numerous seal images and thousands of clay safety devices. It also notes that some sealed documents originated in other cities. A sealing found at Dur-Katlimmu need not have been made there, and the findspot alone cannot identify every seal's place of use.

sections.title: An envelope could repeat the record
sections.text:
TabT05A-151+ from Tell Taban preserves a flour receipt and its envelope. The tablet names the flour, the responsible official Tehup-sheni and the recipient Ashur-ketta-leshir. The envelope repeats those core details. A reader can therefore see how the same transaction existed in both an inner record and an outer covering.

Envelopes also occur with the Tell Taban documents catalogued as purchases of enslaved people. They were part of documentary practice in more than one kind of transaction. The surviving tablet and covering provide concrete evidence of how records were packaged; they do not require us to invent a universal procedure for opening, checking or disputing every envelope.

sections.title: Clay tablets belonged to larger record systems
sections.text:
KAJ 247 mentions a writing-board associated with Sin-ashared as well as the personnel and temple activity recorded on clay. The reference shows that the surviving tablet belonged to a world using more than one writing surface. A clay archive is therefore only part of the original record system, even when its individual transactions remain legible.

Modern publication adds another set of names: KAJ 247 is also identified by museum number VAT 08971 and Oracc/CDLI number P282259. Those labels let readers locate the same ancient object across catalogues and editions. They are modern reference tools, while the ancient names, quantities and date belong to the transaction itself.

title: Temples, ritual texts and sacred institutions
summary: Ashur's sacred kingship, temple labour, offerings and a provincial letter that connects medicine with divination.

sections.title: Ashur linked city, deity and kingship
sections.text:
Ashur was both the name of Assyria's religious and political centre and the name of its principal god. The city contained a sanctuary to Ashur, a temple tower and a royal palace. In the ideology described by Fales, the god authorised a newly enthroned king and charged him with extending the land of Ashur. Territorial rule was consequently presented as a religious responsibility as well as a royal achievement.

That ideology helps explain the prominence of temples in accounts of kingship. A ruler's position was expressed through a relationship to divine authority. It does not tell us what every inhabitant privately believed, but it gives a concrete account of the sacred framework within which royal expansion was justified.

sections.title: A written ritual organised offerings
sections.text:
KAR 139, an Ishtar ritual from Ashur, describes actions by a master of offerings. Its opening directs him into the Bit-eqi and toward a particular position within the ritual setting. Later instructions involve a wooden dish and the pouring of beer from libation bowls into a jar. The ceremony is presented as an ordered sequence of movements and offerings.

The text makes religious practice visible through actions, vessels and a named ritual role. It is more specific than a general statement that Assyrians worshipped many gods. The edition classifies the tablet as Middle Assyrian; its instructions describe a specialist ceremony rather than a complete calendar of worship for all residents.

sections.title: Temples needed organised work
sections.text:
Religious institutions also required personnel and administration. KAJ 247 mentions 22 people, a banquet and activity in a temple under named responsibility. The edition tentatively reads the personnel as corvée workers and tentatively identifies the record as a receipt. Those uncertainties remain important, but the text directly connects a temple setting with the organisation of work.

Cult and supply also meet in the Tell Taban flour account TabT05A-151+. Among its possible purposes is a meal associated with the king's daughter for fourteen days, interpreted in the edition as cultic. The passage's accounting relationship is uncertain. It nevertheless shows why religious history includes food, institutions and resource management alongside prayers and divine names.

sections.title: Medicine and divination could be considered together
sections.text:
In the Middle Assyrian letter TabT05A-134, Lulayu reports an illness and a suggestion that a herb be prescribed. The message also says that the days are not favourable for divination and that extispicy should wait until an appropriate day. Extispicy was divination through examining the internal organs of a sacrificial animal. In this correspondence, practical treatment and attention to auspicious timing appear in the same discussion.

The letter then turns to obtaining medicine or aromatics and asks Labe'tu to send what she has available. It provides a particular provincial example of care, supplies and religious decision-making interacting. It does not establish that every Assyrian illness was treated in the same way.

sections.title: A later biblical account of an Assyrian temple
sections.text:
2 Kings 19:35-37 moves from the destruction of the Assyrian force to Sennacherib's return to Nineveh and his later death. Verse 37 places his killing in the house of Nisroch his god, names Adrammelech and Sharezer as his killers and states that Esarhaddon succeeded him. The passage supplies a biblical account in which an Assyrian king is worshipping when attacked.

That episode belongs to the later Neo-Assyrian kingdom, many centuries after the Middle Assyrian records discussed here. It contributes to the archive's history of Assyrian rulers and worship in its own setting. It should not be used to identify the deity, vessels or ritual sequence of KAR 139.

title: Movement, exchange and regional connections
summary: Letters, flour transfers, sealed records and palace supplies reveal how people and goods connected Middle Assyrian settlements.

sections.title: A kingdom connected by provincial centres
sections.text:
The Middle Assyrian state connected its Tigris heartland with settlements farther west, including Dur-Katlimmu on the Habur. Rule over these areas required communication and supplies to move between places. The provincial centre was a point at which agricultural production, official responsibility and written records could meet.

The surviving documents identify connections more securely than they identify every road. A named destination in an account gives a place within an administrative network; it does not by itself reveal a carrier's exact route. This distinction still leaves a useful historical picture: the kingdom depended on repeated transfers and correspondence linking centres to other settlements, rather than on each city operating alone.

sections.title: Flour was assigned across several demands
sections.text:
TabT05A-151+ from Tell Taban records flour received by Ashur-ketta-leshir from supplies under Tehup-sheni's responsibility. The continuation names the king, Nahur, Kulishhinash, Amasakku and a meal associated with the king's daughter. These references place several locations and purposes within one provincial account.

The wording does not describe a single commercial journey through all those places. In particular, the editor marks uncertainty over how the later uses relate to the received total. The concrete point is that an official receipt could connect locally managed supplies with several institutional demands. Its tablet and envelope retained the transfer's identifying details.

sections.title: Letters co-ordinated supplies and instructions
sections.text:
A letter could arrange a movement before goods changed hands. In TabT05A-134, Lulayu asks Labe'tu to send what she has available for a medical need and says that he will gather what is lacking. He also asks her to send instructions and a greeting. The exchange combines information, requests and a relationship of authority.

This is a specific example of co-ordination across a social network. It makes visible the work of finding supplies and communicating needs. It does not name a market price or establish whether all the materials were bought, held in stores or obtained through another arrangement. Those unanswered details should not replace the information the letter does provide.

sections.title: Palace provisioning could follow constrained people
sections.text:
The footwear receipt MARV 10, 07 gives another kind of connection. A pair of palace shoes was assigned to Niri-shaldi, a hostage, under the great steward Apliya's responsibility. The text mentions the Euphrates and the lands of Tummi and Nairi in a passage tentatively understood as a campaign context.

The receipt places a person under political constraint within the palace supply system. It therefore broadens the subject beyond voluntary trade: movement in an expanding kingdom included officials, military needs and people whose freedom was restricted. The uncertain campaign wording cannot establish Niri-shaldi's precise itinerary, but the named issue of footwear is a concrete administrative act.

sections.title: Sealed documents travelled as well as goods
sections.text:
The Dur-Katlimmu seal study notes that the contents of some tablets point to origins in other cities. A document's place of excavation was therefore not necessarily the place where it was written or sealed. Correspondence and sealed records were themselves objects moving through the kingdom's administrative connections.

That circulation helps explain why one provincial archive can illuminate relationships beyond its own walls. It also distinguishes this evidence from the earlier Old Assyrian merchant correspondence associated with Anatolia. The Middle Assyrian examples here concern provincial supplies, palace responsibility and personal correspondence. They describe their own institutional setting rather than continuing an unchanged form of merchant organisation across centuries.
